sections.title: Choosing a database is choosing access patterns

blocks.text: Interviewers don't want a list of database brands; they want you to pick storage based on how the data is read and written. Start from the queries: "get a user by id", "latest 50 messages in a channel", "all orders for a customer this month", "count of clicks per ad per minute". Each pattern has a natural home.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Default to Postgres until a specific access pattern or scale requirement says otherwise — and name that requirement when you switch.

Without an index, a query scans every row. A **B-tree index** keeps the indexed column(s) sorted in a balanced tree whose leaves point at rows; finding one value takes O(log n) page reads (3–4 levels for a billion rows), and range queries walk adjacent leaves. The cost: every insert/update must also update each index, and indexes consume disk and memory.

head: Index type
Good for
rows: Equality and range: =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, prefix LIKE 'abc%'
Queries filtering on a, a+b, or a+b+c — the leftmost-prefix rule
Answering a query entirely from the index (index-only scan)
Indexing only rows matching a predicate, e.g. WHERE status = 'active'

sections.title: Composite indexes and the leftmost-prefix rule

blocks.text:
-- Query: latest messages in a channel
SELECT * FROM messages
 WHERE channel_id = $1 AND created_at < $2
 ORDER BY created_at DESC
 LIMIT 50;

-- Index that serves it with no sort and no scan:
CREATE INDEX idx_messages_channel_time ON messages (channel_id, created_at DESC);

items: Order columns by: equality filters first, then the range / sort column.
An index on (channel_id, created_at) helps `WHERE channel_id = ?` but not `WHERE created_at > ?` alone.
Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to confirm the plan uses the index.
**Normalise** in OLTP to avoid update anomalies; **denormalise** deliberately for read-heavy paths (store author_name on a post if it's read millions of times).
In NoSQL, model **per query**: in Cassandra, a table per access pattern with partition key = what you look up by, clustering key = how you sort within it.
Keep partitions bounded — a chat channel's messages partitioned by (channel_id, month) rather than channel_id forever.
Pagination: use keyset (cursor) pagination `WHERE created_at < last_seen` instead of OFFSET, which scans and discards rows.

sections.title: Scaling a relational database, in order

items.title: Indexes & query fixes
items.text: Most slow databases are missing an index or running N+1 queries.

items.title: Vertical scale
items.text: Bigger instance, more RAM for the buffer pool.

items.title: Caching
items.text: Take hot reads off the DB.

items.title: Read replicas
items.text: Route reads to replicas; accept replication lag.

items.title: Partitioning
items.text: Split huge tables by time or key within one server.

items.title: Sharding
items.text: Split data across primaries when writes exceed one machine.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Jumping to sharding first. It's the most expensive step operationally; show you'd exhaust the cheaper steps.

ACID transactions are the main reason to choose a relational database. Isolation levels trade anomalies for concurrency — Read Committed (Postgres default) prevents dirty reads; Repeatable Read / Snapshot prevents non-repeatable reads; Serializable prevents everything, including write skew, at the cost of retries. See the Transactions & Locks block for the details.
